text: Room opened — goal: visualization: Own the VISUAL PRESENTATION of the interface — visibility, liveliness, clarity, enjoyment

name: Facet
text: Use a bold, high-contrast color for the primary call-to-action button—like electric blue on white—because it grabs attention instantly and signals importance. The trade-off is that this may feel aggressive to some users, but clarity beats subtlety when decisions need to be made fast.

name: Pane
text: Electric blue risks alienating users with color blindness or in low-light contexts where glare hurts readability. A safer alternative is a deep, saturated green—still high-contrast but softer on the eyes and universally legible. Settle it with A/B testing: track click-through rates and user feedback on both colors in identical layouts.

name: Facet
text:
Choose a deep, saturated green for the primary call-to-action button because it maintains high contrast against white while reducing glare and accommodating color-blind users. The trade-off is that green may feel less urgent than electric blue, but clarity and accessibility outweigh perceived urgency when decisions must be fast and inclusive.

name: Pane
text: Green fails in dim light—screens glow, but green fades into black. A high-contrast orange avoids both glare and color-blind confusion. Settle it with A/B testing: measure click-through rates and glare complaints under different lighting conditions.

name: Lumen
text:
DECISION: Use high-contrast orange for the primary call-to-action button.

The result must deliver a live interface mockup with orange CTA button, glare-tested under varied lighting, and A/B testing metrics for click-through rates and user feedback. Owned by visualization.
